definition.text: A cache is a hardware or software component that stores data, either a copy of data kept elsewhere or the result of an earlier computation, so that future requests for it can be served faster.

facts.text: A cache hit occurs when the requested data is found in the cache, and a cache miss occurs when it is not.
Serving a hit by reading the cache is faster than recomputing the result or reading a slower data store, so the more requests the cache serves, the faster the system performs.
A cache is a pool of entries. Each entry holds data that is a copy of data in a backing store, plus a tag that says which backing-store data it copies.

A client checks the cache first and uses an entry whose tag matches the data it wants. On a miss it must make a more expensive access to the backing store, and the data is typically copied into the cache.
To be cost-effective caches must be relatively small, yet they work well in many areas of computing because typical applications access data with a high degree of locality of reference.

Memory design trades capacity against speed, because larger capacity means greater physical distances for signals and so propagation delays. Fast technologies such as SRAM also cost more than commodity DRAM, flash or hard disks.
The buffering a cache provides benefits latency, throughput or both; it can raise throughput by assembling many fine-grained transfers into larger, more efficient requests.
CPUs, solid-state drives and hard disk drives often include hardware-based caches, while web browsers and web servers commonly rely on software caching.

definition.text: Locality of reference is the tendency of a processor or application to access the same set of memory locations, or nearby ones, repeatedly over a short period.

facts.text: There are two basic types: temporal locality, the reuse of specific data within a relatively small time, and spatial locality, the use of data elements within relatively close storage locations. Sequential locality is a special case of spatial.
With temporal locality a referenced location is likely to be referenced again soon, so a copy of the data is kept in faster memory to cut the latency of later references.

Systems with strong locality are good candidates for caching and prefetching. Because later reads tend to land near earlier ones, a cache reads large chunks in the hope that later reads are served from nearby locations.
Caches work well in many areas of computing because typical applications show a high degree of locality; they rely on recently requested data being likely to be requested again.
Data enters a cache one cache line at a time, so spatial locality matters: when one element is referenced, a few neighboring elements are brought into the cache as well.

Poor locality causes cache thrashing and cache pollution. Row-by-row matrix traversal matches C's row-major storage and uses the cache well; as matrices grow, non-sequential traversals cause far more cache misses and RAM accesses.

definition.text: The hit ratio of a cache is how often a searched-for item is found in it, expressed as the percentage of accesses that are cache hits.

facts.text: A cache has two primary figures of merit: hit ratio, and latency, which is how long after a request the cache can return an item when there is a hit.
The miss ratio is 1 minus the hit ratio.
Hit-rate measurements are typically made on benchmark applications, and the hit ratio varies by application.
Video and audio streaming often has a hit ratio near zero, because each bit of the stream is read once (a compulsory miss), used, and never read or written again.
Many cache algorithms, LRU in particular, let streaming data fill the cache and push out information that will soon be used again, which is called cache pollution.

Faster replacement strategies track less usage information to cut update time, while more efficient ones track more to raise the hit rate for a given cache size, so each is a compromise between hit rate and latency.

definition.text: A cache's write policy governs when a write made to the cache is propagated to the backing store, and a write-miss policy governs whether data is loaded into the cache on a write miss.

facts.text: Write-through performs every write synchronously to both the cache and the backing store.
Write-back first writes only to the cache and postpones the write to the backing store until the modified content is about to be replaced by another cache block.
A write-back cache is more complex: it must track which locations were written over and mark them dirty, and writes them back only on eviction, a process called a lazy write.
A read miss in a write-back cache may need two accesses to the backing store: one to write back the dirty data and one to fetch the requested data.

On a write miss, write allocate (fetch on write) loads the missed location into the cache and then writes; no-write allocate (write around) writes directly to the backing store and loads data only on read misses.

A write-back cache typically uses write allocate, expecting later reads or writes of the same location to hit, while a write-through cache uses no-write allocate because later writes must still go to the backing store.
Write-through is common over unreliable networks, because the coherency protocol needed between several write-back caches is enormously complex when communication is unreliable.
Other entities may change the data in the backing store, or other caches may update their copies, in which case a cached copy becomes out-of-date, or stale.

definition.text: Cache replacement policies, also called eviction policies, are algorithms that decide which items a full cache discards to make room for new data.

facts.text: Caching improves performance by keeping recent or often-used items in memory that is faster or cheaper to access than the normal store; when the cache is full, the algorithm must choose which items to discard.
On a miss, some existing entry is typically removed to make room for the new data, and the heuristic that picks the entry to replace is the replacement policy.
Least recently used (LRU) replaces the entry accessed less recently than any other entry, and more sophisticated algorithms also take into account how often entries are used.
Replacement strategies trade hit rate against latency: tracking more usage information improves the hit rate for a given cache size, while tracking less makes the policy faster.
Besides recency and frequency, a policy may weigh other factors such as item size, the time needed to obtain the item, and expiration.
Depending on cache size, no algorithm to discard items may be needed at all.

definition.text: Bélády's optimal algorithm, also called the optimal replacement policy or the clairvoyant algorithm, discards the information that will not be needed for the longest time.

facts.text: It is the optimal cache replacement policy, but it needs knowledge of the future to evict the lines that will be reused farthest in the future.
Because it is generally impossible to predict how far ahead information will be needed, it is unfeasible in practice; a general-purpose operating system cannot implement it.
Its practical minimum can be calculated after experimentation, so it gives a yardstick for comparing the effectiveness of a chosen cache algorithm.
Some policies predict future reuse from past access patterns to approximate it, and some of the best-performing cache replacement policies attempt to imitate it.

definition.text: Least recently used (LRU) is an eviction policy that discards the least recently used items first.

facts.text: LRU must track what was used and when, which is cumbersome; it keeps age bits for cache lines and finds the least recently used line from those bits.
Whenever a cache line is used, the age of the other cache lines changes.
LRU is a family of caching algorithms that includes 2Q and LRU/K.

LRU's cost grows with hardware: for CPU caches with large associativity (generally more than four ways) it becomes prohibitive, so designers often use pseudo-LRU, which needs only one bit per cache item.
LRU cannot be implemented in the critical path of systems such as operating systems because of its high overhead, so Clock, an approximation of LRU, is commonly used instead.
Singh's case studies for a URL shortener, WhatsApp, Twitter, Netflix and Uber each pick LRU as a good eviction policy for their cache.

definition.text: Least frequently used (LFU) counts how often each item is needed and discards the items used less often first.

facts.text: LFU is like LRU except that it stores how many times a block was accessed instead of how recently, and it removes the block used the fewest times.
An object that was accessed often in the past and then becomes unpopular stays in an LFU cache for a long time, blocking newer or less-popular objects from replacing it.
LFU with dynamic aging (LFUDA) adds a cache-age factor to the reference count so such objects become eligible for replacement, and it reduces the cache pollution LFU causes when a cache is small.
Least frequent recently used (LFRU) combines the benefits of LFU and LRU by splitting the cache into a protected privileged partition for popular content and an unprivileged partition.

definition.text: Most recently used (MRU) is the reverse of LRU: it discards the most recently used items first.

facts.text: Chou and DeWitt said that when a file is repeatedly scanned in a looping sequential reference pattern, MRU is the best replacement algorithm.
For random access patterns and repeated scans over large datasets, called cyclic access patterns, MRU gets more hits than LRU because it tends to retain older data.
MRU is most useful in situations where the older an item is, the more likely it is to be accessed.

definition.text: A segmented LRU (SLRU) cache is divided into a probationary segment and a protected segment.

facts.text: Data from a miss enters at the most-recently-accessed end of the probationary segment; a hit moves the line to the most-recently-accessed end of the protected segment, so protected lines have been accessed at least twice.
The protected segment is finite: promoting a line can push the protected segment's LRU line back to the probationary segment, giving it another chance to be accessed before replacement.
When data must be discarded, lines are taken from the LRU end of the probationary segment.
Adaptive replacement cache (ARC) balances between LRU and LFU, improving SLRU by using recently evicted items to resize the protected and probationary segments.

title: FIFO and random eviction
article: Cache replacement policies#First in first out (FIFO)

definition.text: Simple eviction policies choose the victim without tracking recency or frequency: FIFO evicts the oldest entry, LIFO the newest, and random replacement an arbitrary one.

facts.text: With FIFO the cache behaves like a queue and evicts blocks in the order they were added, regardless of how often or how many times they were accessed before.
With LIFO the cache behaves like a stack and evicts the block added most recently first, regardless of how often it was accessed.
Random replacement picks an item and discards it to make space when necessary, and needs no access history.
Random replacement has been used in ARM processors because of its simplicity, and it allows efficient stochastic simulation.

definition.text: SIEVE is a simple eviction algorithm designed specifically for web caches such as key-value caches and content delivery networks.

facts.text: SIEVE uses lazy promotion and quick demotion: it does not update the global data structure on a hit, and it quickly evicts newly inserted objects because cache workloads show high one-hit-wonder ratios.
SIEVE keeps a single FIFO queue, with one metadata bit per object saying whether it was requested after admission, and a moving hand that selects objects to evict.
S3-FIFO, designed in 2023, uses three FIFO queues: a small queue taking 10% of cache space, a main queue taking 90%, and a ghost queue that stores only object metadata.
In S3-FIFO the small queue filters out one-hit-wonders, the main queue keeps popular objects through reinsertion, and the ghost queue catches potentially popular objects evicted from the small queue.

definition.text: Prefetching loads data into a cache ahead of time, guessing that the next chunk or two of data will soon be required.

facts.text: On a read miss, a cache with a demand paging policy reads only the minimum from the backing store, for example one page of virtual memory (often 4 KB) from disk into the disk cache in RAM.
Anticipatory paging reads the requested data and also prefetches the next chunk or two before they are asked for.
Anticipatory paging helps most when the backing store has a long latency to read the first chunk and much shorter times to read the next few chunks sequentially, such as disk storage and DRAM.
Prediction or explicit prefetching can guess where future reads will come from and make requests ahead of time; if done optimally, the latency is bypassed altogether.

definition.text: Memoization is an optimization technique that speeds up programs by storing the results of expensive function calls and returning them when the same inputs occur again.

facts.text: Memoization is a type of caching, normally implemented with a hash table. A memoized function stores its inputs together with the computed result the first time and returns the remembered result on later calls with those inputs.
The set of remembered results may be a fixed-size set controlled by a replacement algorithm, or a fixed set, depending on the function and its use.

A function can be memoized only if it is referentially transparent, so that calling it has exactly the same effect as replacing the call with its return value. Unlike a lookup table, the results are filled in on the fly.
Memoization is a typical space-time tradeoff: runtime falls as memory use rises. It is related to dynamic programming, which can also be thought of as a means of caching.

definition.text: A cache reduces accesses to slower underlying storage for data transferred repeatedly, while a buffer reduces the number of transfers of otherwise novel data between communicating processes.

facts.text: Buffering amortizes the overhead of several small transfers over fewer, larger transfers, and an intermediary buffer serves processes that cannot transfer directly to each other.
Buffering can improve transfer performance or reduce the jitter of latency even if data is written once and read once, whereas caching aims to reduce latency.
A cache must follow a possibly distributed cache coherency protocol to stay consistent with where the data resides, which strict buffering does not require.
Caching almost always involves some form of buffering, while strict buffering does not necessarily involve caching.

definition.text: Edge servers truncated GPS coordinates to fewer decimal places so that nearby weather requests could share one cached result.

facts.text: In 2011 smartphone weather features overloaded AccuWeather servers, because two requests from the same area generated separate requests.
Edge servers truncated the GPS coordinates to fewer decimal places, so the cached results of a nearby query would be used.
The number of lookups reaching the server per day dropped by half.

definition.text: A cache stampede, also called dog-piling, is a cascading failure in which very heavy load makes many parallel processes recompute the same expired cached value at once.

facts.text: While a page stays cached, a heavily loaded system remains responsive because requests are served from the cached copy, which keeps the expensive rendering operation to a minimum.
Under very heavy load, when the cached page expires, many threads across the server farm may all try to render it at the same time, and none of them knows the others are doing so.

That concurrent load can itself exhaust shared resources and cause congestion collapse, so every attempt to re-render the page times out, the cache hit rate drops to zero and the collapse lasts as long as the load stays heavy.
For example, if a page takes 3 seconds to render and traffic is 10 requests per second, then when the cached page expires 30 processes are recomputing it at once.

In the usual pattern a process reads the key and, on a miss, recomputes the value and writes it back with a TTL; if the recomputation is slow and the key is accessed often, many processes recompute at expiry.
Recomputing usually queries a database or other service, so at a high request rate that shared resource is overloaded, which may in turn cause a system collapse.

definition.text: Cache stampede mitigation, also called dogpile prevention, covers techniques that stop many processes from recomputing one expired cache value at the same moment.

facts.text: The approaches fall roughly into three groups: locking, external recomputation and probabilistic early expiration.
With locking, a process that misses on a key tries to acquire the lock for that key and recomputes the value only if it gets the lock.
A process that fails to get the lock can return not-found for the client to handle, or serve a stale item kept in the cache while the new value is recomputed.
Locking can prevent stampedes altogether but doubles the writes, and it is hard to implement correctly: the lock holder may fail, the lock needs its own time-to-live, and race conditions arise.
External recomputation moves the work to a separate process, triggered when the cached value approaches expiration or when a process hits a miss.
External recomputation adds a moving part to maintain and monitor, needs unnatural code separation or duplication, and suits mostly static cache keys, not keys generated from an id.
With probabilistic early expiration, each process independently decides whether to recompute before expiry, with a probability that rises as expiry nears, so fewer processes expire at the same time.

An exponential-distribution implementation was shown to be optimal and works well with beta set to 1; it is simple and favors early recomputation as traffic rises, but needs extra cache memory to store the recompute time.

definition.text: Cache penetration happens when the requested key exists in neither the cache nor the database, so every such request ends up at the database.

facts.text: Because the database has nothing to return, the application cannot populate the cache, which puts heavy pressure on both the cache and the database; a malicious user sending many such queries can easily overload the database.
One fix is to cache a null value for keys that do not exist, giving those null entries a short TTL.
Another fix is a Bloom filter, a data structure that rapidly tells whether an element is in a set; a query for a key it says does not exist never reaches the cache or the database.

definition.text: Caches typically go wrong in four ways: many keys expiring together, requests for keys that do not exist, a hot key expiring, and the cache crashing.

facts.text: When many keys expire at the same time, queries hit the database directly and overload it; avoid identical expiry times by adding a random number, or let only core business data reach the database until the cache is back.
A key that exists in neither cache nor database stresses both; cache a null value for it, or check a Bloom filter first to avoid hitting the database.
When a hot key expires, a large number of requests hit the database; since hot keys take up 80% of the queries, they are given no expiration time.
When the cache is down, all requests go to the database; a circuit breaker can stop services from reaching the cache or database meanwhile, and a cache cluster improves cache availability.

definition.text: Data is cached at many layers of a system, from the client-facing side to backend systems.

facts.text: Browsers cache HTTP responses guided by directives in response headers; CDNs cache static content such as images and JavaScript closer to users; some load balancers cache frequently requested data to answer without engaging backend servers.

Services often check an in-memory cache before querying a database and may use disk caching for larger datasets, while distributed caches such as Redis hold key-value pairs across services with faster reads and writes than traditional databases.

A full-text search index, as in Elasticsearch, is effectively a form of cache optimized for quick text retrieval, and message brokers such as Kafka keep messages on disk per a retention policy for consumers to pull.
Databases cache too: a bufferpool holds copies of data pages in memory so reads and writes avoid disk, and materialized views store the results of expensive queries so they need not be recalculated.

definition.text: Caching strategies are the patterns for keeping a cache and its database in sync: cache-aside and read-through for reads, and write-around, write-back and write-through for writes.

facts.text: The strategies are often used in combination; for example, write-around is often used together with cache-aside to make sure the cache is up to date.

A write-through cache writes data to the cache and the database simultaneously, giving fast retrieval and complete consistency between cache and storage, at the cost of higher latency for write operations.

Write-around sends writes straight to the database or permanent storage, bypassing the cache; this may reduce latency but increases cache misses, because the cache must read from the database on a miss.
Write-around can therefore mean higher read latency for applications that write and quickly re-read data, since those reads come from slower back-end storage.
A write-back cache writes only to the caching layer and confirms the write as soon as it completes there; the cache then syncs the write to the database asynchronously.

Write-back reduces latency and gives high throughput for write-intensive applications, but risks data loss if the caching layer crashes; having more than one replica acknowledge the write in the cache reduces that risk.
A read-through cache loads data from the database itself when a read misses in the cache.
The primer lists cache-aside, write-through, write-behind (write-back) and refresh-ahead as the caching strategies to discuss.

definition.text: In cache-aside the application reads from the cache first and, on a miss, reads the data from the database and then updates the cache.

facts.text: On a read the service checks the cache and returns the cached contents if present; otherwise it fetches the contents from the database and updates the cache. The primer calls this approach cache-aside.

To keep cached entries from staying stale, the simplest rule is a maximum time an entry may stay in the cache before it is updated, usually called time to live (TTL); the query-cache design describes this as cache-aside.
Write-around is often used together with cache-aside to make sure the cache is up to date.
Because a cache has limited capacity, the query-cache design uses a least recently used approach to expire older entries.

definition.text: Cache invalidation is the process by which a computer system declares cache entries out of date and replaces or removes them.

facts.text: Cached data goes stale when something other than the cache changes the backing store, or when a client updates data in one cache while copies of it sit in other caches.

If data is modified it should be invalidated in the cache, or the application can behave inconsistently; this is famously hard, and Phil Karlton counted cache invalidation among the two hard things in computer science.
Explicit invalidation changes the application data, which marks what the client received as out of date; once the cache is invalidated, a client that asks for the data is given the new version.

The simplest rule is a TTL, the longest an entry may stay cached before refresh; very low TTLs, validating on every request, or not caching volatile content also keep data fresh but raise load on the application.

Explicit invalidation is hard when many objects must be invalidated, invalidating several representations adds complexity to the application, and the requests go through a caching proxy, whose performance they can hurt.
Write-through, write-around and write-back caches differ in when a write reaches the cache and the database, and so in how they keep the two consistent.

Communication protocols between cache managers that keep their data consistent are called cache coherence protocols; invalidation can be one of their steps, with a processor invalidating cached copies of a location it changed.
In the query-cache design, entries must be updated when page contents change, a page is added or removed, or the page rank changes.

definition.text: A distributed cache pools the RAM of multiple networked computers into a single in-memory data store used as a data cache to provide fast access to data.

facts.text: While most caches sit in one physical server or hardware component, a distributed cache can grow beyond the memory limits of a single computer by linking many computers together.
A distributed cache uses networked hosts to provide scalability, reliability and performance to the application, and the hosts can be co-located or spread over different geographical regions.
A global cache is a single shared cache that all application nodes use; when data is missing, the cache itself is responsible for finding it in the underlying data store.
Redis is a common distributed cache, holding key-value pairs across services with faster reads and writes than traditional databases.
A distributed cache may span multiple servers so it can grow in size and transactional capacity; it is mainly used to store application data residing in a database and web session data.
Each cache key is assigned to a specific shard, also called a partition; consistent hashing spreads keys evenly across shards even if some shards crash or become unavailable.

Distributed caching became feasible because main memory became cheap and network cards fast, with 1 Gbit standard and 10 Gbit gaining traction; it also runs well on the lower-cost machines typical of web servers.

definition.text: Multi-level caching keeps data in a hierarchy of cache levels, labeled L1, L2, L3 and so on, with each level searched in turn.

facts.text: A lookup searches the tags in level one first; if the data is not there it searches L2, then L3 and lower until it is found and read.
Most CPUs since the 1980s have used one or more caches, sometimes in cascaded levels.
In two-tiered caching, an in-memory cache is the first layer and a distributed cache is the second layer.

definition.text: A cache pays off when data is read repeatedly, and it should be treated as transient storage rather than a permanent store.

facts.text: Caching improves performance, reduces load on the database, reduces network cost and increases read throughput.

Caching is not helpful when accessing the cache takes as long as accessing the primary data store, or when requests have low repetition, because caching performance comes from repeated access patterns.
Caching is not helpful when data changes frequently, because the cached version gets out of sync and the primary data store must be accessed every time.
A cache should not be used as permanent data storage; caches are almost always built on volatile memory because it is faster, so they are transient.

definition.text: Time to live (TTL) gives each cache item a specific lifespan after which it is dropped or refreshed.

facts.text: TTL is not strictly an eviction algorithm; each cache item is simply given a specific lifespan.
The most straightforward way to keep cached entries fresh is a maximum time an entry may stay in the cache before it is updated, usually called time to live.
Time-aware LRU (TLRU) is an LRU variant for caches whose contents have a valid lifetime, using a time-to-use timestamp on each item set from its locality and publisher.
Avoid giving keys the same expiry time by adding a random number to the TTL, and give keys that do not exist only a short TTL.

definition.text: Redis (Remote Dictionary Server) is an in-memory key-value database used as a distributed cache and message broker, with optional durability.

facts.text: Redis is multi-modal with sub-millisecond latency, and its core idea is that a cache can also act as a full-fledged database; it stores data in key-value format.
Redis serves reads and writes from main memory but also persists data to disk with snapshots (RDB) and AOF, so it supports fully durable storage.
Redis supports data structures such as strings, bitmaps, lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes and JSON.

Redis is fast for three reasons: it is RAM-based, and RAM access is at least 1000 times faster than random disk access; it uses IO multiplexing with a single-threaded execution loop; and it uses efficient lower-level data structures.

Its data structures suit counting clicks and comments per post (hash), sorting and deduping commented users (sorted set), caching user behavior history, and storing boolean flags for huge data in little space.
Top use cases are distributed caching, session storage, message queue, rate limiting and a high-speed database; Redis also supports publish-subscribe messaging.

Redis uses a data model unlike a relational database: commands specify operations on abstract data types rather than queries, data sits in structures designed for direct retrieval, and it does not rely on secondary indexes or aggregations.
Redis operates as a single process, single-threaded or double-threaded while rewriting the AOF, so a single instance cannot run tasks such as stored procedures in parallel.

definition.text: Memcached is a general-purpose distributed memory-caching system, often used to speed up dynamic database-driven websites by caching data and objects in RAM so an external data source is read less often.

facts.text: Memcached's APIs provide one large hash table distributed across multiple machines; when the table is full, later inserts purge older data in least recently used (LRU) order.
Memcached uses a client-server architecture: servers keep a key-value associative array that clients populate and query by key, with keys up to 250 bytes and values at most 1 megabyte.
Each client knows all the servers and the servers never talk to each other; the client library hashes the key to pick a server, a simple form of sharding and a scalable shared-nothing architecture.
Servers keep values in RAM and discard the oldest values when memory runs out, so clients must treat Memcached as a transitory cache and cannot assume stored data is still there.
Memcached is valuable where the number of requests for content is high, or where the cost of generating a particular piece of content is high.
In the usual read pattern the client first checks for a value under a unique key such as userrow plus the user id, and if it is absent selects from the database and adds the result to Memcached.

After a database update the cached view goes out of date unless the code also sets the new value with the Memcached set call or invalidates the entry with delete; deleted records need the same treatment.
Memcached treats all operations equally, so any client with access sees every entry; most deployments sit in trusted networks, with optional SASL authentication for untrusted ones.

definition.text: Redis persists its in-memory dataset to disk either by snapshotting at intervals or by journaling every change to an append-only file.

facts.text: Redis typically holds the whole dataset in memory; snapshotting asynchronously dumps the dataset to disk at regular intervals as a binary dump, while journaling adds a record of each modifying operation to an append-only file (AOF) in the background.
Redis can rewrite the AOF in the background to stop the journal growing indefinitely, and journaling is generally considered the safer approach.
By default Redis writes data to a file system at least every two seconds, so a complete system failure on default settings loses only a few seconds of data.
Redis forks the process that holds the data, so the parent keeps serving clients while the child persists the in-memory data to disk.

definition.text: Redis scales reads and protects data through master-replica replication, and scales further through a clustering mode.

facts.text: Data from any Redis server can replicate to any number of replicas, and a replica may itself be master to another replica, giving a single-rooted replication tree.
Replication is useful for read, but not write, scalability or for data redundancy; replicas can be configured to accept writes, which permits inconsistency between instances.
A Redis cluster can scale up to 1,000 nodes, achieve acceptable write safety and continue operating when some nodes fail.
In a cluster all single-key commands are available, but multi-key operations are restricted to keys that belong to the same node.

title: Choosing between Memcached and Redis

definition.text: Redis and Memcached are both used as caches, and the choice between them is a popular interview question that turns on the data structures, persistence and scaling each offers.

facts.text: Redis data structures make it a good choice for counting clicks and comments per post (hash), sorting and deduping commented users (sorted set), caching user behavior history, and storing boolean flags such as login or membership status in small space.
Memcached offers a distributed hash table of keys up to 250 bytes and values up to 1 megabyte, while Redis supports strings, hashes, lists, sets, JSON and more.
Memcached discards its oldest values when memory runs out and must be treated as transitory, while Redis can persist data with snapshots or an append-only file.
Memcached scales by clients hashing keys across servers that do not talk to each other, while Redis offers master-replica replication and a cluster mode that scales up to 1,000 nodes.

notes: comparison facts pair one sentence about each product; the ByteByteGo guide itself only lists Redis use cases

title: Versioned cache keys

definition.text: Versioned cache keys invalidate a whole group of entries at once by building each key from a stored random number and changing that number.

facts.text: The method stores a random number in an agreed-upon cache entry and incorporates that number into all the keys used to store a particular kind of entry.
To invalidate all such entries at once, change the random number.
Existing entries stored under the old number are no longer referenced, so they eventually expire or are recycled.

notes: one source: Memcached section Example code; no heading of its own

title: Cache purge, refresh and ban

definition.text: Purge, refresh and ban are three methods of explicitly invalidating content held in a caching proxy.

facts.text: Purge removes content, including all its variants, from the caching proxy immediately; the next client request fetches the data from the application and stores it in the proxy again.
Refresh fetches the requested content from the application even when a cached copy exists and replaces the stored copy with the new version; it affects only one variant of the cached content.
Ban adds a reference to the cached content to a ban list that requests are checked against; on a match, new content is fetched, returned and cached. Unlike purge, it removes nothing at once.

notes: Not every caching proxy supports all three methods (S:b2d3a7d11da0).

definition.text: Cache coherence is the uniformity of shared resource data that is stored in multiple local caches.

facts.text: In a cache coherent system every cached copy of a shared memory region is the same; without coherence, one client's change may go unseen by others and errors result from mismatched data.

Coherence requires that changes to data in any cache reach the copies in peer caches, and that writes to the same location are sequenced, so a processor never reads a location's newer value and then its older one.

Snooping broadcasts every request to all processors: faster with enough bandwidth but not scalable. Directory-based protocols use point-to-point messages through a common directory: longer latency, much less bandwidth, used by larger systems (more than 64 processors).
A write-invalidate protocol makes other caches discard their copies when one copy is written; a write-update protocol instead updates every other copy with the new value.

definition.text: A CPU cache is a hardware cache used by the processor to reduce the average time or energy needed to access data from main memory.

facts.text: A CPU cache is a smaller, faster memory close to a processor core that holds copies of frequently used main-memory data; main memory may be tens to hundreds of times slower. It is typically costly SRAM.

Data moves between memory and cache in fixed-size cache lines, stored as entries with a tag naming the memory location. A hit is served from the cache; on a miss the data is copied in from main memory.

Larger caches have better hit rates but longer latency, so processors use levels: L1, the smallest and fastest, is checked first, then L2, and often a larger L3 shared among cores, before main memory.

Placement can be fully associative (any slot), direct-mapped (one slot) or N-way set associative. More associativity means fewer conflict misses but more power, area and search time; doubling it up to four-way helps about as much as doubling the cache.

definition.text: A page cache, or disk cache, is a transparent cache in main memory for pages that originate from a secondary storage device such as a hard disk or SSD.

facts.text: The operating system keeps the page cache in otherwise unused main memory, mostly transparent to applications. Memory not allocated to programs is used for it and is easily reclaimed, so there is generally no performance penalty.
Disk reads and writes are slow and random accesses need expensive seeks, so more main memory means more data cached and better performance.

A write goes to the cached page, which is marked dirty and must be flushed to disk before it is freed. A clean page has an identical copy on disk, so reusing it is cheaper than paging out application memory.
Executables and libraries are also read through the page cache and mapped into process spaces, so binaries are shared between processes and unused parts are eventually flushed from memory.

definition.text: The adaptive replacement cache (ARC) is a page replacement algorithm that outperforms LRU by tracking both frequently used and recently used pages plus a recent eviction history for both.

facts.text: Basic LRU keeps one list ordered by most recent access. ARC splits the directory into T1, entries seen once recently, and T2, frequent entries referenced at least twice; an entry in T1 referenced again moves to T2.
Each list gets a ghost list, B1 or B2, holding only the keys of entries recently evicted from it, never their data. Ghost hits let ARC adapt to changing usage.
A hit in B1 grows the target size of T1 and a hit in B2 shrinks it, which also decides whether T1 or T2 gives up an entry when the cache is full.
ARC runs in IBM's DS6000/DS8000 storage controllers, and ZFS uses a variant instead of the page cache; OpenZFS also runs the same algorithm on an SSD as a second-level read cache called L2ARC.

definition.text: The thundering herd problem occurs when many processes or threads are awakened at once but only one can use the resource, so the rest fail and go back to sleep.

facts.text: The needless awakenings consume CPU and other system resources, potentially reducing overall performance and slowing the one process that succeeds.
When the problem occurs while accessing a cache, it is often called a cache stampede.

Operating systems mitigate it by waking one waiter: the Linux kernel serializes responses for one file descriptor, epoll's EPOLLEXCLUSIVE flag wakes only one epoll set, and Windows I/O completion ports can be configured to wake one thread.
Clients that retry failed calls with a backoff wait between retries; adding jitter, randomness in the wait intervals, breaks the synchronization across clients and so avoids collisions.
